q-rc-detail.label: A fact the passage states
q-rc-detail.summary: 'According to the passage ...': the answer is a line you can point to.

q-rc-main.label: Main idea or key distinction
q-rc-main.summary: What the passage is mostly about; the idea that most of its sentences support.

q-rc-inference.label: Implied meaning or reason
q-rc-inference.summary: A reason or implication that follows from what is said but is not word for word in the passage.

q-rc-remedy.label: Cause, remedy or deciding factor
q-rc-remedy.summary: What causes a problem, what the author suggests to fix it, or what decides an outcome.

rules.text: The answer is in the passage. Take one key word from the question, find it in the passage, and read that sentence. An option that is true in general but not in the passage is wrong.
rules.ok: Question: who has wisdom without schooling? Passage: farmers, craftsmen and elders.
rules.bad: Choosing 'policy analysts' because it sounds sensible.

rules.text: For an implication, stay close to the passage's own direction: the correct option extends a stated idea (wisdom is the moral use of knowledge), while wrong ones introduce a new topic (language, numbers) or reverse a stated one.
rules.ok: 'Wisdom enriches the soul' -> it nurtures moral understanding.
rules.bad: Choosing 'numerical ability', which the passage never mentions.

rules.text: A remedy or decisive factor is announced by signals such as 'The cure is', 'the antidote', 'depends on', 'essential'. Find that sentence and choose the option that restates it.
rules.ok: 'The cure is to build dissent into the system' -> encouraging constructive dissent.
rules.bad: Choosing 'strict compliance', which makes the problem worse.

rules.text: An option can repeat the passage's own words and still be wrong, because it changes the claim: it swaps the cause for the effect, turns one example into the whole point, or states as fact what the author only allows as possible. Match the claim, not the vocabulary.
rules.ok: Passage: sealed ground sends rain to drains. Option: sealed ground stops recharge.
rules.bad: Option: drains cause the monsoon to fail (same words, new claim).

rules.text: The main idea is the one claim every paragraph is working for. Test an option by asking whether the passage would collapse without it; an option that only one paragraph supports is a detail, not the main idea.
rules.ok: A passage on why groundwater keeps falling and what would stop it.
rules.bad: 'Borewells are cheap to drill', which is one sentence of it.

q-rc-detail.cue: 'According to the author / As per the passage ...' with a who, what or which question.
q-rc-detail.standard: Pick one key word from the question, find it in the passage, and read that sentence. Choose the option that restates it.
q-rc-detail.fast: Skim the passage once for names, numbers and lists; they are where details sit.
q-rc-detail.eliminate: Cross out options naming things the passage never mentions.
traps: Options that sound sensible but are not in the passage.
Mixing up two cases that appear close together.

q-rc-main.cue: 'What key distinction / main point / central idea ...'
q-rc-main.standard: Read the first and last sentences, then ask what idea every paragraph supports.
q-rc-main.fast: The first sentence often states the contrast the whole passage develops.
q-rc-main.eliminate: Drop options that cover only a small part of the passage or a different topic.
traps: An option that names one example, not the central point.
A broad option about the subject but not the passage's own point.

q-rc-inference.cue: 'What is implied by ...', 'Why does the author describe ... as ...'
q-rc-inference.standard: Find the sentence nearest the idea, then pick the option that follows from it without adding new facts.
q-rc-inference.fast: Look for the option that uses the passage's own key words (moral, ethical, both reliable and false).
q-rc-inference.eliminate: Remove options from a different area or that reverse the author.
traps: An option that is true but not implied.
An option about a neighbouring topic (language, numbers).

q-rc-remedy.cue: 'What remedy', 'what factor decides', 'what has contributed to ...'
q-rc-remedy.standard: Look for 'the cure is', 'depends on', 'as a result' and read the sentence around it.
q-rc-remedy.fast: The last two sentences of a paragraph usually state the remedy or the deciding factor.
q-rc-remedy.eliminate: Drop options that make the problem worse or are unrelated to the author's suggestion.
traps: An option that sounds like a remedy but is the opposite of what the author wants.
A factor named in the passage but not as the cause the question asks for.

education-wisdom.title: Education and wisdom
education-wisdom.src: Our own condensed restatement of the passage in the SSC CGL Tier-I similar paper of 12 Sep 2025 (Adda247, shift 1). Not the original text.
education-wisdom.text: People often use 'education' and 'wisdom' as if they meant the same thing, but they do not. Education is the organised gathering of knowledge, proved by degrees and marks and delivered through set courses and examinations. Wisdom goes further: it is the careful and moral use of what one knows in real situations, and it grows out of experience, self-reflection, emotional intelligence and a sense of right and wrong. A highly educated person can still lack wisdom if learning never turns into good judgement or responsible action, while farmers, craftsmen and elders, who may have little schooling, often show great wisdom because their choices rest on lived experience. Education sharpens the mind; wisdom deepens understanding. In an age of information overload and algorithm-driven thinking, the gap has widened. Schools tend to reward rote learning, exam scores and standard results, sometimes at the cost of critical thinking, ethical reasoning and emotional maturity, so society turns out people who solve technical problems well but struggle to decide with empathy, patience and foresight. Wisdom cannot be downloaded, rushed or certified. It comes slowly through trial and error, failure and reflection. Education usually ends with a qualification, whereas wisdom is a lifelong pursuit, shown in humility, steady ethical conduct and the calm handling of uncertainty. The best intelligence, in the end, is not only knowing what is right but acting on it even when that is hard.

social-media-democracy.title: Social media and democracy
social-media-democracy.src: Our own condensed restatement of the passage in the SSC CGL Tier-I similar paper of 12 Sep 2025 (Adda247, shift 2). Not the original text.
social-media-democracy.text: Social media has changed democratic life deeply: it encourages public participation, yet it also carries strategic deception. Platforms that began as places for personal sharing are now major arenas of political talk, where citizens voice opinions, gather around causes and hold the powerful to account almost at once. Because democracy relies on ideas and information moving freely, these platforms widen access by loosening the hold of traditional gatekeepers. Leaders can speak to voters directly, and citizen-led movements can use viral momentum to bring neglected concerns into public view, so during elections, protests and policy disputes they work like a digital marketplace of ideas. But the openness is risky. The networks that spread accurate information also speed up falsehoods, deepen polarisation and harden echo chambers through algorithms. Fake profiles, coordinated harassment and organised disinformation have disturbed elections in several democracies, and content built to stir emotion and maximise engagement often drowns out careful reasoning. So the effect on democracy depends not only on technology but on the ethical rules governing its use. Strong oversight, public media awareness and transparency about how algorithms rank and recommend content are essential if societies want the benefits without the damage. Social media is neither automatically good nor bad; it reflects collective choices, and the outcome depends on how responsibly citizens, institutions and platforms use it.

groupthink.title: Groupthink and conformity
groupthink.src: Our own condensed restatement of the passage in the SSC CGL Tier-I similar paper of 12 Sep 2025 (Adda247, shift 3). Not the original text.
groupthink.text: Groupthink arises when a team's wish for total agreement outweighs its willingness to examine other views critically. Decisions then become flawed, because disagreement is silenced from inside or discouraged by social cost. Related to it is social conformity, the habit of adjusting one's opinions or behaviour to match the majority, often without noticing, to win acceptance or avoid friction. In close circles such as boardrooms, policy groups and academic committees, people may hold back opposing ideas for fear of exclusion or damage to their reputation. Over time this uniformity breeds mental stagnation, weakens creativity and raises the risk of strategic mistakes. The Bay of Pigs episode and the Challenger space shuttle disaster are widely cited as classic cases in which groupthink distorted judgement. Psychologically, conformity is linked to an evolutionary pull towards tribal belonging, when standing apart could threaten survival. Today the same impulse appears as peer pressure, workplace norms and online echo chambers. Digital platforms intensify conformity because their algorithms build personalised bubbles that confirm what people already believe and filter out conflicting views. The cure is to build dissent into the system: when teams welcome principled disagreement, it acts as a safety check against tunnel vision, and valuing counterviews instead of punishing them supports stronger, more balanced decisions. Real progress comes not from automatic loyalty to majority norms but from critical probing and the nerve to challenge what feels comfortable.

city-groundwater.title: The water under the city
city-groundwater.src: Written by us for practice. Not from any paper.
city-groundwater.text: Most Indian cities now drink from the ground. Piped supply reaches only part of the population and runs for a few hours a day, so households, builders and factories sink their own borewells and pump as much as they need. Nobody meters this water and nobody owns it in common, which means the cheapest way to secure supply is to drill deeper than the neighbour. The result is a slow race downwards. In parts of the Deccan the water table has fallen by more than thirty metres in two generations, and shallow wells that once served whole villages now stand dry for nine months of the year. What makes the fall hard to reverse is that the city has also sealed its own soil. Roads, car parks and concrete roofs shed rain into drains instead of letting it soak in, so even a good monsoon recharges very little. A city can therefore flood in July and run short of water in April, and residents see no contradiction between the two events because they are told that the first is a drainage problem and the second a supply problem. Engineers have offered the obvious answers for decades: harvest rain where it falls, keep ponds and tanks open instead of building on them, treat and reuse waste water, and meter what is pumped. Few of these are expensive. They fail for a simpler reason: the benefit of restraint is shared by everybody while the cost is paid by whoever restrains first. Until pumping is measured and priced, the rational act for each household remains the one that ruins the aquifer for all of them. The way out is not a new technology but a change of ownership. Where village councils and resident groups have been given legal charge of a defined aquifer, together with the right to see the data and to set limits on their own members, extraction has fallen without anybody being policed from outside.

machines-work.title: Machines that learn, and work
machines-work.src: Written by us for practice. Not from any paper.
machines-work.text: When a new machine can do a task that people were paid to do, two things happen at once, and arguments about technology and employment usually confuse them. The first is displacement: the particular job disappears or shrinks. The second is reinstatement: cheaper output, higher incomes and new goods create demand for work that did not exist before. Both effects are real, and which one dominates is a question of fact in a given decade, not a matter of optimism or pessimism. History offers no single verdict. Mechanised spinning destroyed hand spinning and then employed far more people in weaving, finishing and selling cloth than the old craft ever had. Automatic telephone exchanges, by contrast, removed the switchboard operator and created almost nothing in her place. What is different about systems that learn from data is the breadth of what they touch. Earlier machines took over physical motion or arithmetic. The present ones take over pattern recognition, and pattern recognition is the core of a great deal of skilled office work: reading a scan, drafting a contract, marking an examination, answering a complaint. The workers exposed are therefore not the least educated but the moderately educated, and they are many. Two things decide how that lands. One is the speed of the change, because an economy can absorb over thirty years a displacement that would break it in five. The other is who holds the gains: if the saving goes entirely to the owners of the system, demand does not rise enough to pull displaced workers into new jobs, and the reinstatement effect never arrives. This is why the useful policy questions are dull ones: how quickly skills can be rebuilt in mid-career, how income is taxed and shared, and whether a worker can move between jobs without losing a pension or a house.

sleep.title: Sleep is not idleness
sleep.src: Written by us for practice. Not from any paper.
sleep.text: Sleep looks like the absence of activity, and for most of the twentieth century it was studied as if it were one: a pause during which the body waited for morning. The recordings tell a different story. The sleeping brain is not quiet but busy in a particular order, and the order matters more than the total. Deep slow-wave sleep, most of which comes in the first half of the night, is when the brain clears the waste that builds up while we are awake and when the body does most of its repair. Rapid-eye-movement sleep, which lengthens towards morning, is when the day's experience is replayed and filed, and when loose facts are stitched into something that can be used later. A student who studies until three and then sleeps for five hours does not lose a flat fifth of the benefit; she loses most of a stage, because the stage she cuts is the one that was due last. This is why the common remedies disappoint. Caffeine does not add sleep, it only hides the pressure to sleep, and the pressure returns with interest. Sleeping pills shorten the time taken to fall asleep but suppress the deep stage, so the night is longer and emptier. Catching up at the weekend restores alertness and mood but repairs memory poorly, because the material has already been consolidated badly or not at all. What does work is unglamorous and nearly free. A fixed waking time anchors the body clock more firmly than a fixed bedtime does. Morning light advances that clock and evening screens delay it. A cool, dark room lengthens the deep stage. The reason the advice is ignored is cultural rather than medical: we treat short sleep as evidence of seriousness, and so the one habit that improves attention, mood and memory together is the one we boast about skipping.

gig-work.title: The bargain of by-the-hour work
gig-work.src: Written by us for practice. Not from any paper.
gig-work.text: A platform that matches a rider to a delivery does something genuinely new: it lets a person work for an hour without being hired for a year. For many that flexibility is worth a great deal, whether a student between classes, a parent in school hours, or a man holding a second job together with a first. The exchange is not a swindle, and it is not charity either; it is a bargain, and both of its sides are worth stating plainly. What the worker gains is control over time and an income that starts on the first day, with no interview and no notice period. What the worker gives up is everything that used to come bundled with employment: a floor under the hourly rate, payment when there is no work to be had, a share of a pension, cover when he is injured on the road, and somebody to appeal to when a decision goes against him. The last of those is the sharpest, because pay and allocation are set by software that neither explains itself nor hears an argument. A rider whose account is suspended over a complaint he never sees has lost his job without a hearing, and the law in most countries does not recognise the loss as a dismissal because it does not recognise him as an employee. The usual proposals pull in two directions. One would declare such workers employees and hand them the whole bundle, which is clean in law but would end the by-the-hour flexibility that drew many of them in. The other would leave the contract alone and let competition protect them, which assumes that a worker can switch platforms as easily as a platform can replace a worker. A third way is less tidy and more promising: attach the protections to the hours worked rather than to the status of the worker, so that cover and contributions follow a person across platforms.

forest-rights.title: Forests and the people in them
forest-rights.src: Written by us for practice. Not from any paper.
forest-rights.text: The idea that a forest is best protected by removing the people who live in it has an orderly look and a long record of failure. It entered Indian law in the nineteenth century, when woodland was reclassified as state property in order to secure timber for railways and ships, and the villagers who had grazed, gathered and burnt in it became trespassers on land their families had used for centuries. The trees were not saved. What was created instead was a boundary that nobody living beside it had any reason to respect. Conservation science has since caught up with what the foresters' own records already showed. A forest is not a museum exhibit but a disturbed system: grazing, lopping and small controlled fires keep grassland open, spread seed and clear the fuel that would otherwise feed a crown fire. Where such use stopped abruptly, scrub closed in, the animals the reserve had been built for moved out, and the first dry summer carried a fire nobody could stop. The alternative is not an absence of rules. It is rules made and enforced by the people who stand to lose if the forest goes. A village that holds a recognised right to a patch of bamboo has an interest in its regrowth that no patrol can manufacture; the same village, declared an encroacher, has an interest only in cutting the bamboo before somebody else does. What still obstructs this is administrative rather than ecological. Recognising a right requires the state to record who holds it, which is slow, contested and politically awkward, while a boundary and a guard can be ordered in a week. The cheap instrument is therefore chosen again and again, and its failures are blamed on the people it excluded.

Because they are concentrated in factories
practice.why: Earlier machines took over motion and arithmetic; these take over pattern recognition, and that is what much skilled office work consists of.

a.note: Cost of replacement is never given as the reason; the kind of work is.

b.note: Willingness to retrain is not discussed, only how quickly skills can be rebuilt.

d.note: The exposed tasks listed, such as reading a scan and drafting a contract, are office work, not factory work.

practice.evidence: pattern recognition is the core of a great deal of skilled office work

practice.text: Which two things, according to the author, decide how the change lands?
options: The quality of the machines and the size of the market
The speed of the change and who keeps the gains
The level of schooling and the rate of interest
The number of jobs lost and the number of firms founded
practice.why: The passage names the speed of the displacement and the question of who holds the saving, because without rising demand the reinstatement effect never arrives.

a.note: Neither machine quality nor market size is named.

c.note: Schooling appears only in the description of who is exposed, and interest rates are never mentioned.

d.note: These are measures of the outcome, not the two deciding factors the passage names.

practice.evidence: One is the speed of the change

practice.text: What does the author imply about the usual arguments over technology and jobs?
options: They are settled by the historical record
They confuse two different effects and treat a factual question as a matter of temperament
They are driven by the interests of machine owners
They matter less than the pace of invention
practice.why: The passage says such arguments usually confuse displacement with reinstatement, and that which one dominates is a question of fact, not of optimism or pessimism.

a.note: The passage says history offers no single verdict, so the record does not settle it.

c.note: Who holds the gains is raised as one factor in the outcome, not as the motive behind the arguments.

d.note: The pace of invention is not weighed against the arguments anywhere in the passage.

practice.evidence: arguments about technology and employment usually confuse them

practice.text: What is the central claim of the passage?
options: Eight hours of sleep is the correct amount for an adult
Sleep is structured activity, and the order of its stages matters more than the total
Caffeine and sleeping pills are dangerous drugs
Students should not study late at night
practice.why: The passage replaces the idea of sleep as a pause with sleep as ordered activity, and says the order matters more than the total.

a.note: No total is ever recommended; the passage argues the total is not the main thing.

c.note: Caffeine and pills appear as remedies that disappoint, which is a step in the argument, not its claim.

d.note: The student is an illustration of losing a whole stage, not the subject of the passage.

practice.evidence: the order matters more than the total

practice.text: Which stage, as the passage describes it, clears waste and does most of the body's repair?
options: Rapid-eye-movement sleep
The first few minutes of drowsiness
Deep slow-wave sleep
The period of catching up at the weekend
practice.why: Deep slow-wave sleep, mostly in the first half of the night, is when waste is cleared and the body does most of its repair.

a.note: Rapid-eye-movement sleep is described as the filing of experience, not as waste clearance or repair.

b.note: Falling asleep is mentioned only in connection with sleeping pills.

d.note: Weekend catching up is described as restoring alertness but repairing memory poorly.

practice.evidence: Deep slow-wave sleep, most of which comes in the first half of the night, is when the brain clears the waste

practice.text: Why does a student who sleeps five hours lose more than a fifth of the benefit?
options: Because five hours is below the medical minimum
Because the stage that is cut is the one due last, and it is lost almost entirely
Because studying late raises the pressure to sleep
Because the deep stage cannot begin before midnight
practice.why: Rapid-eye-movement sleep lengthens towards morning, so cutting the end of the night removes most of one stage rather than a slice of each.

a.note: The passage names no medical minimum; its argument is about which stage is lost.

c.note: The pressure to sleep is raised in connection with caffeine, not with the student.

d.note: No clock time is given for the deep stage, only that it falls in the first half of the night.

practice.evidence: she loses most of a stage, because the stage she cuts is the one that was due last

practice.text: What does the passage say actually works?
options: A fixed waking time, morning light and a cool, dark room
A fixed bedtime enforced with a mild sedative
Catching up on sleep at the weekend
A device that tracks the stages of sleep
practice.why: The passage calls the working habits unglamorous and nearly free: a fixed waking time, morning light rather than evening screens, and a cool, dark room.

b.note: The passage says a fixed waking time anchors the clock more firmly than a fixed bedtime, and that pills suppress the deep stage.

c.note: Weekend catch-up is listed among the remedies that disappoint, because it repairs memory poorly.

d.note: The passage says none of what works requires a device.

practice.evidence: A fixed waking time anchors the body clock more firmly than a fixed bedtime does

practice.text: Why does the author think the advice is ignored?
options: It is too expensive for most people
It contradicts the medical evidence
Short sleep is treated as proof of seriousness
It has only recently been discovered
practice.why: The passage calls the reason cultural rather than medical: short sleep is treated as evidence of seriousness, so people boast about skipping it.

a.note: The passage says what works is nearly free, so cost is not the reason.

b.note: The advice comes from the recordings, so it does not contradict the evidence.

d.note: The passage dates the mistaken view to the twentieth century but does not call the advice new.

practice.evidence: we treat short sleep as evidence of seriousness

practice.text: What is the passage mainly doing?
options: Condemning delivery platforms as exploitative
Setting out both sides of the by-the-hour bargain and proposing a third way
Explaining how software allocates deliveries
Advising students on part-time work
practice.why: The passage says plainly that the exchange is neither a swindle nor charity but a bargain, states what is gained and given up, and then proposes attaching protection to hours worked.

a.note: The passage explicitly refuses that reading: it says the exchange is not a swindle.

c.note: The software is mentioned to explain why the loss of appeal is the sharpest cost, not as the subject.

d.note: Students are named once as people for whom flexibility is worth a great deal.

practice.evidence: it is a bargain, and both of its sides are worth stating plainly

practice.text: Which of these does the passage list among the things the worker gives up?
options: Control over his own working hours
Cover when he is injured on the road
An income that starts on the first day
The freedom to hold a second job
practice.why: The list of what is given up includes a wage floor, payment when there is no work, a pension share, cover for injury on the road, and a right of appeal.

a.note: Control over time is on the other side of the bargain: it is what the worker gains.

c.note: An income starting on the first day is also listed as a gain, not a loss.

d.note: Holding two jobs is given as a reason the flexibility is valued.

practice.evidence: cover when he is injured on the road

practice.text: Why does the author call the loss of someone to appeal to the sharpest cost?
options: Because riders rarely know the rules of the platform
Because an unexplained suspension ends the job without a hearing and the law does not count it as dismissal
Because appeals are expensive to file
Because platforms change their pay rates frequently
practice.why: Pay and allocation are set by software that neither explains itself nor hears an argument, so a suspended rider loses his job without a hearing and the law does not treat it as a dismissal.

a.note: Knowledge of the rules is not the issue; the absence of any hearing is.

c.note: The cost of filing an appeal is never mentioned.

d.note: Changing pay belongs to the earlier list of what is given up, not to this point about appeal.

practice.evidence: has lost his job without a hearing

practice.text: What third way does the passage propose?
options: Declaring every platform worker an employee
Leaving the contract alone and trusting competition
Attaching protections to the hours worked so that they follow the worker across platforms
Setting a national minimum rate for every delivery
practice.why: The passage proposes tying cover and contributions to hours worked rather than to employment status, so that they follow a person from platform to platform.

a.note: That is the first of the two proposals the passage sets aside, because it would end the by-the-hour flexibility.

b.note: That is the second proposal, which the passage says rests on a false assumption about switching.

d.note: A national minimum rate is not among the proposals discussed.

practice.evidence: attach the protections to the hours worked rather than to the status of the worker

practice.text: What objection does the author raise to leaving the contract alone and relying on competition?
options: Platforms would collude to fix rates
It assumes a worker can change platforms as easily as a platform can replace a worker
Competition would push rates above what customers would pay
Workers do not understand the contracts they sign
practice.why: The passage says that proposal assumes a worker can switch platforms as easily as a platform can replace a worker, which is the weakness in it.

a.note: Collusion between platforms is never raised.

c.note: The effect on customers is not discussed.

d.note: Understanding the contract is not the objection; the imbalance in the power to walk away is.

practice.evidence: assumes that a worker can switch platforms as easily as a platform can replace a worker

practice.text: What does the passage chiefly argue?
options: Forests should be left entirely alone
Forests are better protected by the people who live in them than by exclusion
Indian forest law was written to supply railway timber
Controlled fires are the main tool of conservation
practice.why: The passage argues that excluding residents has a long record of failure and that rules made by those who lose if the forest goes work better.

a.note: The passage says the alternative is not an absence of rules, and that use keeps the system healthy.

c.note: The timber motive is the historical opening of the argument, not its claim.

d.note: Fire is one of several uses listed as keeping grassland open, not the main point.

practice.evidence: It is rules made and enforced by the people who stand to lose if the forest goes

practice.text: Why was woodland reclassified as state property in the nineteenth century?
options: To settle disputes between neighbouring villages
To secure timber for railways and ships
To create reserves for wild animals
To raise revenue from grazing fees
practice.why: The passage says woodland became state property in order to secure timber for railways and ships.

a.note: Village disputes are not mentioned as a motive.

c.note: Reserves for animals come later in the passage, when use had already stopped.

d.note: Grazing is mentioned as a use that was criminalised, not as a source of revenue.

practice.evidence: woodland was reclassified as state property in order to secure timber for railways and ships

practice.text: Why did scrub close in where the villagers' use stopped?
options: Because rainfall increased after the reserves were created
Because grazing, lopping and small fires had been keeping the grassland open
Because the reserves were planted with new species
Because the animals that ate the scrub were hunted out
practice.why: The passage treats the forest as a disturbed system in which grazing, lopping and controlled fire keep grassland open; when that use ended abruptly, scrub closed in.

a.note: Rainfall is not mentioned at all.

c.note: Planting is not mentioned.

d.note: Animals are said to have moved out after the scrub closed in, so they are the consequence, not the cause.

practice.evidence: grazing, lopping and small controlled fires keep grassland open

practice.text: What, according to the passage, still obstructs recognised local rights?
options: Evidence that local management harms forests
The administrative difficulty of recording who holds a right
The opposition of conservation scientists
The absence of any law allowing such rights
practice.why: The passage calls the obstruction administrative rather than ecological: recording who holds a right is slow, contested and politically awkward, while a boundary and a guard can be ordered in a week.

a.note: The passage says the pattern of success has been recorded often enough to be unsurprising.

c.note: Conservation science is said to have caught up with this view, so it is not the obstacle.

d.note: The passage does not say the law is missing; it says recognition is administratively hard.

practice.evidence: Recognising a right requires the state to record who holds it, which is slow, contested and politically awkward

practice.text: What does the author imply by saying a boundary and a guard can be ordered in a week?
options: That enforcement is the cheapest way to save a forest
That the state repeatedly picks the quick instrument over the one that works
That guards are better trained than village councils
That boundaries are drawn without maps
practice.why: The sentence contrasts the speed of ordering a boundary with the slowness of recognising rights, and the passage then says the cheap instrument is chosen again and again.

a.note: The passage calls it cheap but gives it a long record of failure, so it is not presented as a way to save a forest.

c.note: The training of guards is never discussed.

d.note: How boundaries are drawn is not discussed.

practice.evidence: The cheap instrument is therefore chosen again and again
